title: Alys Bumble's Best Glow
markdown:
In Whispering Willows, nestled among rolling green hills, the air smelled of honeysuckle and bread. The year's great fuss was the village pageant: dazzling costumes, delightful performances, and Aunt June's famous fizzy lemonade. For weeks the children practiced lines and sewed sequins until their fingers ached. The grown-ups baked, decorated, and fussed until the hall looked like a captured rainbow.

This year a different tingle ran through the lanes. Alys Bumble wanted to join in. Alys was a dragon, very big, very polite, scales the color of sunset, eyes as round and earnest as a startled owl's. He adored the willow-whisper, Mrs. Higgins's honey cakes, and village chatter. He tried so hard to be considerate that his best intentions had a habit of arriving with a spotlight attached.

Luca the raccoon, moonlight fur, tail twitching at every new idea, was helping decorate and scanning for fun. Tansy the rabbit smoothed Luca's mischief when she could; her whiskers quivered, and her fluffy tail drooped when chaos climbed too high. Aunt June, a badger of considerable age and even more considerable kindness, hummed as she pinned streamers.

"Now, Luca," she said, voice like moss after rain. "No glitter in the punch. Last year Mrs. Gable's prize cat looked like a disco ball for a fortnight."

Luca grinned until his face crinkled. "It was festive. A whole village twinkling."

Tansy nudged him. "Be good. Besides — I heard Alys Bumble is going to carry the banner."

"Alys Bumble?" Luca scoffed without meanness. He liked Alys. The idea of Alys doing anything without a hullabaloo was simply too funny. "He'll hold it so nobly he walks into a tree. Or breathe on it by accident."

The procession proved Luca half right, which was his favorite fraction.

The air buzzed. Villagers lined the cobbles, faces alight. Alys was given the honor of the very large Welcome to Whispering Willows banner — magnificent, gold thread, tiny painted flowers. He held it with such immense care, stretching it so perfectly straight and tall, that he towered over the ancient oaks lining the route, his head nearly in the clouds. Villagers craning their necks saw a sliver of embroidery, a few painted petals, and then Alys's eager face above it, like a polite moon.

"He's practically a mountain," someone whispered, awed.

Alys blushed pink across sunset scales. "Oh, thank you!" he boomed, trying for modest. A dragon's polite boom still rattled Mrs. Higgins's teacups. Smaller children giggled and pointed at the sky-holder.

Next, the talent show. A group of squirrels, dressed in tiny velvet waistcoats, performed a synchronized acorn-juggling routine, paws a blur, catches remarkable. The audience clapped and cheered. Then Alys decided he wanted to participate. He had practiced with great diligence: a gentle puff of smoke to float dandelion seeds through the air, subtle and charming, like a fairy tale that knew when to stop.

"It's just a little puff," he murmured to Mayor Bumbleton, whose spectacles were already sliding from stress. "An ethereal effect."

He took a deep gentle breath and puffed.

It was not a little puff. It was a pearly grey weather system. It swallowed the stage, the squirrels, the acorns, and half the front row. When it cleared, the squirrels looked as if they had sprouted temporary fluffy wings. They chittered and batted. Alys stood in a halo of leftover smoke, terribly pleased with his subtlety.

Luca shook with silent laughter. "Well. Fog."

Aunt June patted heads. "He means well. Being the loudest whisper is still being the loudest. And Alys's whispers are resonant."

The grand tableau was a reenactment of the founding of Whispering Willows. Main parts went to villagers in elaborate costumes on a rustic stage. This year the benevolent founder — a wise old badger with a long beard and a twinkle — was to be played by Alys. He was to stand tall and noble, overlooking the scene, a silent inspiring presence, which in theory required no fire at all.

"Now, Alys," pleaded Penelope Featherbottom, the pageant director, a frazzled chicken whose clucks had gone desperate. "Just stand there. Don't do anything. A noble statue."

Alys nodded, earnest as dawn. He waited behind the boards for Professor Hoot's cue. The dignified owl began the settlers' tale. Alys, wishing to look inspiring, puffed his chest, gave a majestic slow nod, and let out a tiny, almost silent glow from his nostrils. A guiding star, he thought.

The tiny glow was brighter than a thousand fireflies. It lit the square like noon, warped the moonlit scene, froze the actors mid-pose, and left Professor Hoot's beak hanging. The tableau washed out. All eyes found Alys, accidentally radiant, still trying to be a statue.

Luca and Tansy shared a glint. Aunt June saw the performers' faces, Penelope fanning herself with a program, Professor Hoot sighing as if the founding had been a personal insult.

"Hmm." Aunt June leaned toward the children. "He wants to belong. He doesn't know how to be large without filling the whole picture. We should find him a job where bigness and brightness help, instead of bleaching everyone else."

Luca's whiskers twitched. He nudged Tansy. "What if his best part isn't being the brightest light, but helping the other lights work?"

They scurried to Alys, who looked confused by the silence.

"Alys," Tansy said, a breeze in the grass. "You were magnificent. Luminous. A magical sunbeam."

"But," Luca added, urgent in the theatrical way, "the pageant is about all of us. Penelope just remembered — she needs someone to settle the stars for the finale." He gestured at the shy first stars, and at the dim fairy lights strung between the willows.

Alys blinked. "The stars? I haven't any tools. And they're very high."

"You have better." Luca tapped his snout. "When you blow very gently, like a summer wind, you can wake those little tree-lights. Tuck them in with your breath. Make them twinkle their best. No smoke. No noon. Just air."

Alys's eyes widened. He loved tucking things in. He loved soft breezes. He shuffled to the square's edge, where the fairy lights looked dim and a bit sorry. He took a deep, controlled breath and exhaled the softest sigh — not smoke, not glare, a whispered lullaby to wire and glass.

The lights shivered awake, brighter, a starlit canopy. Villagers gasped, this time in the useful kind of awe. The tableau people could see one another's faces. The finale went on, splendid, under a glow Alys had coaxed instead of drowned.

He watched, warmth in his chest that had nothing to do with fire. He was not the middle of the picture. He was why the picture could be seen. The gentle wind of his breath seemed to coax the best out of every little lamp, and the founder-badger (now played, hastily, by a villager who fit the beard) could be noble at a human height.

When the pageant ended, they cheered the performers, Aunt June's unsparkling lemonade, and the polite dragon who had at last found a considerate size for his shine. Alys beamed, a happy smile that did not require sunglasses. Children still pointed, but they pointed at the canopy now, which was what he had hoped for in the first place, before he had tried to be a mountain, a fog bank, and a second sun.

Luca, who would still put glitter in punch given half a chance, admitted that fairy lights were a superior sparkle. Tansy's tail un-drooped. Aunt June poured lemonade and did not make a speech; the square, twinkling, was doing that work.

Alys looked up at the strings, still dancing.

"I wonder," he said, modest as a mountain practicing indoor voice, "whether next year I might be in charge of the breeze for the streamers — and leave the founder to someone who fits behind a beard."

Penelope Featherbottom clucked, faintly, in relief. Professor Hoot closed his beak. The willows, which had whispered all along, sounded, for once, as if they approved.
characters: Alys (polite dragon), Luca (raccoon), Tansy (rabbit), Aunt June (badger)
